lead: Ethereum development needs a safe chain to compile, deploy and test contracts before real ether is at risk. A development environment is the editor, compiler, EVM and connection tools you use. A test network is a public chain with valueless ether. A private net is your own chain with your own genesis. These tools catch bugs, check gas and rehearse deployment before mainnet.
prereq: You need: contract lifecycle in 5.4, Solidity in 5.5, and mining and consensus in Unit 3.

blocks.text: A development environment is all the software used to write, compile, deploy, call and debug a contract. Remix IDE runs in a browser. It has an editor, a Solidity compiler, a deploy panel and a debugger. It can run a JavaScript VM in the browser, so a contract deploys in seconds without a node. It can also connect to an injected wallet or to a node RPC URL.

items: Local blockchain tools such as Ganache, Hardhat Network and Anvil start a chain on your laptop. They mine on demand and give funded test accounts.
Use local tools for automated tests and quick resets. Use a public testnet when other people or services must reach your contract.

blocks.text: A testnet is a public Ethereum network with ether that has no market value. Sepolia is a common testnet. Testnet names and endpoints change, so never trust an old tutorial. A faucet is a service that sends a small amount of test ether to your address. It may require a sign-in or a proof of work. Test ether lets you pay gas without risking rupees.

Testnets share Ethereum rules but not mainnet state. A contract address on Sepolia is not the same contract on mainnet. The address can look the same, but the state and balance belong to that chain. The chain ID inside transactions keeps signatures from being replayed on another chain. See 5.2 for transaction fields.

Some syllabi call this Ethereum development environment, test networks and setting up a private net. A private net is a chain you control. It has its own genesis block, its own chain ID and its own accounts.

items: Write a genesis file. It sets config.chainId to 1337, gasLimit to 30,000,000, and an alloc entry that gives account A, whose key you hold, 100 ETH. The chain ID is used in transaction signatures. The alloc gives starting balances before block 1.
Initialize the data directory: geth init genesis.json --datadir ./mynet. This writes the genesis block into that directory. A different genesis file creates a different chain.

Start the node with the same data directory and a network ID, for example --networkid 1337. The network ID groups peers; the chain ID from genesis signs transactions. Turn on HTTP RPC only on 127.0.0.1 for local work. Turn on mining if your client version supports it; on some local dev chains blocks are produced on demand.
Create account B with geth account new or import a key. Unlock account A locally so it can sign a transaction. Never unlock a mainnet account on a public RPC.
Send 1 ETH from A to B with gas limit 21,000 and gas price 1 gwei. The transaction enters the pending pool.
Mine block 1. The transaction is included, A pays 1 ETH plus the fee, and B receives 1 ETH. Query both balances to confirm.

blocks.text: A transfer of ether between two externally owned accounts costs 21,000 gas. Gas is the unit of work; gas price is ether per gas. The fee is:

blocks.where: fee is in ETH; gas used is in gas units; gas price is in ETH per gas. 1 gwei = 0.000000001 ETH.

blocks.text: The block gas limit is the maximum gas all transactions in a block may use. It does not set your fee. A gas limit on a transaction is a cap; unused gas is refunded. The miner receives the fee. In the worked example, block rewards are ignored because they do not change A or B.

A pending transaction has no balance change. A wrong chain ID or a different genesis gives a different network, not a connection to mainnet. Test ether is only for testing and has no market value. See Unit 3, Proof of Work and mining, for why a block must be mined.

figure.caption: A sends 1 ETH at 21,000 gas and 1 gwei, so the fee is 0.000021 ETH. Mining block 1 commits the transfer: A ends with 98.999979 ETH and B with 1 ETH.

spec.title: Private net: genesis to block 1
spec.aria: Private net flow: genesis sets chainId 1337 and gives A 100 ETH, geth init loads it, the node starts with networkid 1337, B is created and A unlocked, A sends 1 ETH at 21,000 gas and 1 gwei, the transaction stays pending with no balance change, mining block 1 charges a 0.000021 ETH fee, and final balances are A 98.999979 ETH and B 1 ETH.

examples.question: A private net genesis sets chainId 1337 and block gas limit 30,000,000. Account A starts with 100 ETH in genesis. A sends 1 ETH to B using 21,000 gas at 1 gwei. Ignoring block rewards, find A and B balances after mining.
steps: Gas used = 21,000 gas. Gas price = 1 gwei = 0.000000001 ETH per gas.
Transaction fee = 21,000 × 0.000000001 ETH = 0.000021 ETH. This is 21,000 gwei.
A starts with 100 ETH. A sends 1 ETH to B and pays 0.000021 ETH fee: 100 − 1 − 0.000021 = 98.999979 ETH.
B receives the transfer only. B = 0 + 1 = 1 ETH. The fee goes to the miner, not to B.
The block gas limit 30,000,000 is above 21,000, so the transaction fits. It does not change the fee. Ignoring block rewards, final balances are A = 98.999979 ETH and B = 1 ETH.
examples.answer: After block 1 is mined, A has 98.999979 ETH and B has 1 ETH.
examples.check:
from decimal import Decimal
gas_used = Decimal(21000)
gas_price_gwei = Decimal(1)
eth_per_gwei = Decimal('0.000000001')
fee = gas_used * gas_price_gwei * eth_per_gwei
a_start = Decimal(100)
transfer = Decimal(1)
a_final = a_start - transfer - fee
b_final = transfer
print(float(a_final))
print(float(b_final))

traps: Test ether has no market value. If a site sells test ether, treat it as a warning. Faucets give small amounts for testing only.
A wrong chain ID or genesis file creates a different network. It does not connect to mainnet. The same address on two chains has separate balances and state.
Do not confuse gas limit with fee. A 21,000 gas transfer at 1 gwei costs 0.000021 ETH. A block gas limit of 30,000,000 is only a block cap.
A pending transaction is not a balance change. If mining is off, the transfer stays pending and balances do not move.
Testnet names, RPC URLs and faucets change. Check the chain ID before sending a transaction; an old tutorial may point to a dead or different network.

quiz.a: A public Ethereum-like network with valueless ether used for testing contracts and transactions.

quiz.q: Name two local blockchain tools used in Ethereum development.
Why is Remix's JavaScript VM faster than a public testnet for a first deploy?
quiz.a: It runs in the browser and keeps state locally, so there is no peer propagation, faucet wait or public block time.

quiz.q: A private genesis gives A 100 ETH. A sends 2 ETH at 21,000 gas and 2 gwei. Ignoring block rewards, find A's balance.
Find the fee for 21,000 gas at 3 gwei in ETH.
Why can the same address show different balances on Sepolia and mainnet?
quiz.a: They are separate chains with separate state. The address is derived from a key, but balance and contract storage are stored per chain; chain ID stops replay.

quiz.q: A student starts geth with a different genesis file but the same network ID and expects to join mainnet. Explain the error.
quiz.a: The genesis block defines the chain. A different genesis makes a separate private chain. A matching network ID does not merge it with mainnet; peers must share the same genesis and chain rules.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern teams use Hardhat or Foundry with fork testing, where a local chain copies mainnet state at a chosen block. CI pipelines start a fresh chain per test run, deploy contracts and record gas. Layer-2 testnets and short-lived devnets are now common. Search for Foundry Anvil fork, Hardhat network forking and Ethereum testnet faucet to go further.
